nameStory: Prairie cordgrass gets its name from its natural home on the Great Plains prairies, where it forms vast stands in wet meadows and sloughs. The "cord" part refers to its tough, rope-like stems that early settlers found difficult to cut through, requiring special tools to harvest.
description: Prairie cordgrass is a tall, robust perennial grass that can tower 4-8 feet high, forming dense colonies through underground runners. Its long, narrow leaves arch gracefully from sturdy stems, creating an almost fountain-like appearance. In late summer, it produces distinctive flower clusters that look like narrow, feathery plumes. This is one of our most impressive native grasses, built to thrive in wet soils where other plants might struggle.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow leaves up to 3 feet long with razor-sharp edges that can actually cut your finger if you run it along the blade - handle with care! The leaves have a distinct bluish-green color and feel quite stiff and leathery.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense colonies through creeping underground stems, often creating large patches of uniform height. Individual stems stand very straight and rigid, rarely bending even in strong winds.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Produces narrow, spike-like flower clusters in late summer that are initially purplish, then fade to tan. The flower heads are much more compact and less feathery than many other tall grasses.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, hard seeds that drop easily when ripe, making a subtle rattling sound when you shake dried seed heads in fall and winter.

habitat: Look for prairie cordgrass in wet meadows, freshwater marshes, ditches, and along pond edges throughout New England. It thrives in areas that are seasonally flooded or consistently moist, often growing alongside cattails, sedges, and other wetland plants. You'll rarely find it in dry upland areas.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge bright green in late spring, growing rapidly once the soil warms. Young leaves are less sharp than mature ones.
seasonality.summer: Reaches full height by midsummer with distinctive blue-green foliage. Flower spikes appear in late summer, initially purplish and quite showy.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn golden-yellow to tan, and seed heads ripen to a warm brown color. Seeds begin dropping by early fall.
seasonality.winter: Persistent tan stems and seed heads remain standing, creating striking winter silhouettes. The rigid stems rarely break or bend under snow.

funFact: Prairie cordgrass is so tough that early settlers called it "ripgut" because it could slice through clothing and skin, and it was notorious for dulling the blades of mowing equipment - some farmers had to use special serrated sickles just to cut through it!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with big cordgrass, but prairie cordgrass has much sharper leaf edges and grows in freshwater areas, while big cordgrass prefers brackish marshes. Remember: "prairie" = freshwater and razor-sharp leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name, prairie cordgrass isn't limited to prairies - it's actually quite common in New England's wetlands. The scientific name was recently changed from Spartina pectinata to Sporobolus michauxianus, so you might see it listed under either name in field guides.
compareHints: Among its Sporobolus relatives in New England, prairie cordgrass is by far the tallest and most robust. Saltmarsh cordgrass grows in salt marshes rather than freshwater, while the dropseed species are much smaller and grow in dry, sandy areas rather than wet habitats. Prairie cordgrass also has the sharpest leaf edges of any grass in this group.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Sporobolus relatives in New England, Saltmarsh Cordgrass is the giant of the group and the only one that thrives in salt water.
Unlike its relative Saltmarsh Cordgrass which grows tall and sturdy in the lowest marsh zones, Marsh Hay Cordgrass is shorter and more delicate, preferring slightly higher ground.
Big Cordgrass towers over its Sporobolus relatives - Saltmarsh Cordgrass and Marsh Hay Cordgrass rarely exceed 3 feet tall and have much finer, more delicate appearances.
Unlike its coastal relatives like saltmarsh cordgrass and marsh hay cordgrass which are robust perennials of salt marshes, poverty dropseed is a small annual of dry, sandy inland areas.
Unlike its Sporobolus relatives in New England (the cordgrasses), sand dropseed lives in dry, sandy inland areas rather than salty marshes.
